verdicts.why: Applying a law or rule names the act of enforcement without any attitude toward it.
Applying oneself to a task is a plain description of directed effort, not praise or blame.
Applying a word or name to something is a neutral act of reference.
Applying to a person or body for something is the plain, even formal, word for making a request.
Saying a rule or analysis applies states relevance and carries no judgement.
Applying paint or a compress is a physical act with no attitude attached.
Giving notice of withdrawal is a neutral, formal term for the notification itself.
A posted notice is simply a sign; the word takes no side on it.
A notice in the sense of a short review names a kind of text, not an opinion of it.
A notice requesting payment is a plain document name; the unwelcome referent is not a loaded word.
An effect of a drug or illness is a neutral name for a symptom, with no attitude beyond the meaning.
A law being in effect is a legal-status term that describes without judging.
Words to that effect names the gist of a statement neutrally.
Inviting someone to attend is the plain word for the request and carries no judgement of either party.
Inviting criticism or comparison states that conduct makes an outcome likely; the object may be bad but the verb itself does not judge.
Inviting someone in is a plain description of asking them to enter.
Expressing willingness to have a guest is neutral hospitality vocabulary.
Having someone as a guest is described without any attitude toward host or guest.
Changing clothes is a plain everyday action with no evaluative load.
Exchanging one thing for another of the same kind is neutral description.
Changing sides or one's mind names the act of switching without approving or condemning it.
Changing places or words with someone is a neutral reciprocal exchange.
Changing trains or buses is a plain travel term.
Changing a bed or a baby names replacing coverings and carries no attitude.
A voice changing at puberty is a neutral description of the physical shift.
